note: Nine original questions, no private Moodle original wording; review record only, not live bank.

items.stem: In deterministic planning, what makes a sequence of actions a valid plan?
choices: It reaches a goal-satisfying state from the initial state using applicable actions
It lists every possible state without selecting actions
It predicts only a probability of success
It has no defined goal
items.explanation: A valid plan applies legal actions to reach a goal state.
items.teaching_locator: Automated Planning lecture, initial and goal states

items.stem: In forward state-space planning, what do graph nodes and directed arcs represent?
choices: Training examples and model weights
World states and applicable actions leading to other states
Workers and their wages
Dates and arbitrary labels
items.explanation: Nodes represent states and arcs represent applicable action transitions.

items.stem: A planner finds a valid plan without proving it has minimum total cost. What has been established?
choices: The task is infeasible
The plan is proven optimal
A satisficing plan has been found
The plan is necessarily the most expensive
items.explanation: Satisficing means valid without a proof of cost optimality.

items.stem: What is the principal role of a heuristic in state-space planning?
choices: To replace all action preconditions
To enumerate every future observation
To guarantee optimality under every search algorithm
To estimate remaining effort or cost and guide search
items.explanation: Heuristics guide search; optimality depends on the algorithm and heuristic conditions.

items.stem: Tasks A and B must precede C, but neither precedes the other. What does a standard topological sort provide?
choices: A dependency-respecting order, possibly A-B-C or B-A-C
Proof that A must always precede B
All possible valid orders in one standard sort result
An optimized one-worker schedule
items.explanation: One dependency-respecting ordering is returned; it is not resource optimisation or all orderings.

items.stem: What does sampling uncertain task durations from a probability distribution accomplish?
choices: It proves the fastest adaptive policy
It represents uncertainty without automatically optimizing a contingent policy
It makes all real-world durations deterministic
It removes all precedence constraints
items.explanation: Simulation of uncertain outcomes does not by itself prove an optimal adaptive policy.
items.teaching_locator: Automated Planning lecture, probabilistic planning and Pyro

items.stem: How does hierarchical task-network planning refine a complex goal?
choices: It assigns a single random action
It ignores all dependencies
It decomposes compound tasks into subtasks until executable actions remain
It only trains a classifier
items.explanation: HTN planning decomposes compound tasks into subtasks and primitive actions.

items.stem: Which scenario best represents complex problem solving in the account of Dörner and Funke (2017)?
choices: A fixed one-step calculation
An evolving system with interacting variables, incomplete information and competing goals
A routine task with no feedback
A task without human judgment
items.explanation: Complexity involves dynamic interdependence, opacity and competing goals.
items.teaching_locator: Dörner and Funke (2017), Innovation reading added 2026-10-15

items.stem: What do Fahrbach and Fust (2026) propose to support complex-problem-solving expertise?
choices: Memorise a fixed response
Avoid metacognitive reflection
Combine planning, monitoring and evaluation with motivational and metacognitive regulation
Treat a theoretical proposal as proof of universal effectiveness
items.explanation: The paper proposes an SRL conceptual framework, not demonstrated universal efficacy.
items.teaching_locator: Fahrbach and Fust (2026), Innovation reading added 2026-10-15
